findings.title: INSERT feed_items (skip duplicates) builds one statement from every row of SELECT follows by followee_id
findings.consequence: The VALUES list grows with the result of an unbounded query. Postgres accepts at most 65,535 parameters per statement, so once the list is big enough (with 2 parameters per row, past 32,767 rows) the INSERT fails outright, and anything written before it in the same request stays written.
findings.fix: Let the database do it in one statement (INSERT ... SELECT ... FROM the source table), or insert in fixed-size batches, ideally in a transaction or a background job.

findings.title: EXISTS then DEL on refresh:<userId>:<jti>: two steps, not one
findings.consequence: Two requests with the same key can both pass the EXISTS before either runs DEL. If the key is a one-time token (a refresh token, a reset code), both requests succeed with it, which is exactly what one-time use is meant to prevent.
findings.fix: Make the check and the change one command: use DEL's result as the check (it returns 1 only for the caller that actually deleted the key), or GETDEL, or a Lua script.

findings.title: bcrypt.compare competes for libuv's 4 threads
findings.consequence: Hashing runs off the main thread, but on a pool of only 4 threads by default. It uses the cost stored in the hash, 12 where this repo hashes, so each one takes roughly 260 ms (an estimate; it depends on the CPU), so one process handles about 15 hashes per second, shared by every route that hashes or checks passwords before POST /api/auth/login start queueing for a thread. File reads and DNS lookups (for example a new database connection) wait behind them too.
findings.fix: It's already rate-limited (10r/s per client IP at the proxy and 20 per 15 min per client), which stops one client from hammering it but not a real peak of many users. Raise UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE (to about the number of CPU cores), run more instances, or move hashing to a separate worker pool.

insights.explanation: Ids are UUID columns, but route params such as /api/posts/:id go straight into SQL, so a non-UUID value makes Postgres throw an error that has no statusCode. The error middleware then returns 500 and sends err.message, the raw Postgres text, to the client. The same thing happens with a tampered pagination cursor (decodeCursor only checks that both halves exist) and with values longer than a column allows, such as a bio over 150 characters. insights.title: Postgres published on the host with default credentials
insights.explanation: The app container is only exposed on the internal Docker network, but the postgres service maps port 5432 on the host with user and password postgres/postgres. Anyone who can reach the host can connect as the superuser and read or change every table, bypassing nginx, the rate limiters and the app. Redis, by comparison, is not published.

insights.title: Register, login and refresh share one per-IP limit
insights.explanation: A single authLimiter instance is mounted on all three routes, so they share one Redis counter per client IP: 20 requests per 15 minutes in total, successful ones included. Token refreshes use up the login budget, and many users behind one NAT or office IP can lock each other out. The limit is per IP only, so an attacker who rotates IPs is never limited per target account.
